content: 1. A study published in Neurourology and Urodynamics in 2015 (Volume 34, Issue 4, Pages 300–308) analyzed specific aspects of care for older adults. Another review by Soriano et al. in Clinical Interventions in Aging (2007, Volume 2, Issue 4, Pages 545–553) focused on falls among community-dwelling older adults, providing guidance for primary care providers. 2. Gillespie et al. conducted a systematic review on interventions to prevent falls in older adults living in the community, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2012 (Issue 9, Article CD007146). The World Health Organization (WHO) also released a global report on fall prevention in older age, emphasizing the importance of tailored interventions. 3. Fortin et al. discussed the challenges of managing multimorbidity in older adults in a 2007 article in the BMJ (Volume 334, Pages 1016–1017). Similarly, Alzheimer’s Disease International and WHO highlighted the need to support informal caregivers of individuals with dementia during the first WHO Ministerial Conference on Global Action Against Dementia in 2015. 4. Douglas et al. evaluated the impact of disease management programs on caregivers of critically ill patients in a study published in Chest (2005, Volume 128, Issue 6, Pages 3925–3936). Shaw et al. conducted a systematic review of respite care for frail elderly individuals, published in Health Technology Assessment in 2009 (Volume 13, Issue 20, Pages 1–224). 5. Sorensen et al. updated a meta-analysis on the effectiveness of interventions for caregivers, published in The Gerontologist (2002, Volume 42, Issue 3, Pages 356–372). Mason et al. examined the cost-effectiveness of respite care for caregivers of frail older adults in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society (2007, Volume 55, Issue 2, Pages 290–299). 6. Valentijn et al. proposed a conceptual framework for integrated care based on primary care functions in the International Journal of Integrated Care (2013, Volume 13, Article e010). Curry and Ham emphasized clinical and service integration as a pathway to improved outcomes in a report accessed in 2017. 7. Goodwin et al. explored coordinated care for individuals with complex chronic conditions in a WHO report. The WHO also published a 2015 global reference list of 100 core health indicators, emphasizing the importance of integrated, people-centered health services. 8. The WHO Collaborating Centre at the University of Geneva, along with other international institutions, contributed to the development of guidelines for integrated care for older adults. These guidelines addressed various health challenges, including mobility loss, undernutrition, vision and hearing impairments, cognitive decline, depression, urinary incontinence, and fall prevention. 9. The guideline development process involved managing conflicts of interest among group members. For example, Professor Olivier Bruyère, a member of the European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis, declared no significant conflicts. Similarly, Dr. Alan Dangour disclosed receiving a grant for research on nutrition in older adults, which was deemed minor. 10. Professor Matteo Cesari, who had affiliations with Nestlé, was partially excluded from decision-making related to nutritional supplementation guidelines. Other experts, such as Dr. Nandi Siegfried, provided technical support without participating in closed sessions. 11. The guidelines addressed specific interventions for older adults, such as physical exercise for mobility loss, oral nutritional supplements for undernutrition, and case-finding for vision and hearing impairments. Psychological therapies were recommended for depressive symptoms, while non-pharmacological interventions were suggested for urinary incontinence. 12. Fall prevention strategies included multicomponent exercise programs, medication reviews, and environmental modifications. Caregiver support interventions, such as respite care and psychosocial support, were also evaluated for their benefits. 13. The guideline development process involved systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and quality assessments using tools like AMSTAR and GRADE. Evidence was synthesized to inform recommendations, ensuring methodological rigor and transparency. 14. The final guidelines emphasized the importance of integrated care for older adults, addressing critical health outcomes such as mobility, nutrition, sensory impairments, cognitive function, and caregiver well-being.
